exact_claim: On 7 October 1892, in Munich, Max von Pettenkofer drank a cholera culture
source_1: S2 Mendelsohn 2001 (7 Oct 1892, Munich)
primary_source: P1 Pettenkofer, as translated in J Hyg 1901 ('On the 7th of October, 1892 ... I took this cholera-drink'); P2 BMJ 19 Nov 1892 ('October 7th')
notes: Say: 'Munich, 7 October 1892.' Never frame as a stunt to copy.

exact_claim: He was 73 years old (born 3 December 1818)
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 ('Der 73-Jährige')
source_2: L1 Wikipedia (born 3 Dec 1818, Lichtenheim near Neuburg); P1 J Hyg 1901 (born 1818 near Neuburg)
notes: Say '73' or 'in his seventies'. His own text says 'I am 74 years old' (P1): only use 74 inside his quote.

exact_claim: He described himself as old and frail: 74, glycosuria for years, not a single tooth left
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 translation of his account; P2 BMJ 1892 ('74 years old, glycosuric, without a tooth in his head')
notes: Good character beat: 'an old man with no teeth'. Attribute: 'he wrote'. 'Diabetic' is a modern gloss of glycosuria: say 'sugar in his urine' or skip.

exact_claim: His theory: the cholera germ alone is not enough; an epidemic also needs local conditions (polluted porous soil, falling groundwater) and personal predisposition (his x, y, z)
source_1: S3 Morabia 2007 (germ transformed by dry porous soil when groundwater is low)
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 (x / y / z); P1 J Hyg 1901 obituary
notes: Say: 'He believed germs alone could not cause cholera. The soil and the ground water had to be right too.' Do NOT say he denied germs exist: he accepted the comma bacillus as one factor.

exact_claim: His rival Robert Koch held that the comma bacillus causes cholera and spreads through contaminated drinking water
source_1: S6 Roy Porter, LRB 1987 (Koch identified the vibrio in Hamburg's drinking water)
notes: Koch found the bacillus in 1883-84 (Egypt / India; sources give either): don't state a year on screen.

exact_claim: In 1892 cholera killed about 8,600 people in Hamburg (8,605)
source_1: S8 Manson, Tropical Diseases 1919 (8,605 deaths; 13.4 per 1,000)
source_2: S9 Evans, Death in Hamburg 1987 (about 8,600 deaths; via German ed. and secondary summaries)
notes: Say 'about 8,600 people died' or 'thousands died'. Porter's '10,000' is a rounding: don't use.

exact_claim: Neighbouring Altona drew from the same river Elbe but filtered its water, and had only 328 cholera deaths
source_1: S8 Manson 1919 (Altona 328 deaths, 2.1 per 1,000; 'most carefully filtered')
source_2: NPR 2020 / Darden blog citing Evans (Altona filtered, Hamburg did not)
primary_source: Koch 1893, 'Wasserfiltration und Cholera', Z Hyg 14 (not seen)
notes: Optional context beat. Altona was a separate town, not 'a street' unless you show the boundary street (S8 confirms a street formed the boundary in one part).

exact_claim: He drank it in front of witnesses
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 ('vor Zeugen')
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 translation ('in the presence of witnesses')
notes: Names of the witnesses at the drinking: see C27 (UNKNOWN).

exact_claim: The culture: a broth (bouillon) culture made in Munich by Drs Pfeiffer and Eisenlohr from pure agar cultures of the comma bacillus made by Professor Gaffky; less than 24 hours old
source_1: P2 BMJ 1892 (via S4 Burnett reprint)
source_2: P3 Pettenkofer, Arch Hyg 18 (1893) pp.116-117: bacilli 'aus Hamburg stammenden', 'vollvirulent'
primary_source: P2 BMJ 19 Nov 1892; P3 Arch Hyg 1893
dispute_status: origin disputed in popular accounts (see C11)
notes: Say: 'a fresh culture of cholera germs from the Hamburg outbreak'. Full chain (Gaffky -> Munich broth) can go in the description.

exact_claim: Georg Gaffky was Koch's former assistant and in 1892 advised the government on the Hamburg epidemic
source_1: S11 G. Robinson, Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Encyclopedia.com)
source_2: RKI edoc: Gaffky reports 'Cholera in Hamburg 1892-1893' (24 Sep and 2 Oct 1892)
notes: Allows a fair line: 'germs grown by one of Koch's own men'. Don't say Koch sent them.

exact_claim: Koch himself sent him the culture (or: it was ordered from Koch's Berlin institute)
source_1: L1 Wikipedia ('from Koch')
notes: Primary record says Gaffky's cultures, from Hamburg. Do not say 'Koch sent it'.

exact_claim: He first neutralised his stomach acid: 1 gram of bicarbonate of soda in 100 cc of Munich tap water, about two and a quarter hours after a light breakfast
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901 ('after neutralising with soda the contents of the stomach')
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892
notes: Say: 'He even drank baking soda first, so his stomach acid couldn't kill the germs.' No amounts on screen (copy risk).

exact_claim: He took the bicarbonate to answer Koch's point that stomach acid kills the bacteria
source_1: L1 Wikipedia
notes: Only Wikipedia (unreferenced) links it to Koch. BMJ just says 'to neutralise the acid'. Don't name Koch here.

exact_claim: The dose: 1 cubic centimetre of the culture, swallowed at a draught; he then rinsed the glass with 50 cc of water and drank that too
source_1: S4 Burnett 2009 (reprint of BMJ)
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892
notes: Visual: a tiny amount at the bottom of a glass. Say 'one cubic centimetre of pure cholera culture' or 'a small glass'. Never 'a whole glass'.

exact_claim: The culture held about one billion cholera germs
source_1: S12 Huxley (popular)
notes: Not in BMJ / J Hyg. Pettenkofer only mused on 'milliards' in his stools afterwards. Say 'billions' only if attributed to his own estimate; safer to say 'a huge dose'.

exact_claim: He drank 'a whole glass' of cholera culture
notes: It was 1 cc plus a water rinse.

exact_claim: He wrote that the cholera drink 'tasted like the purest water'
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 translation of his account
notes: Strong line. Attribute: 'He wrote that it tasted like pure water.' English is a 1901 translation; German original (MMW 1892) not seen.

exact_claim: Some of his friends / pupils offered to take the risk in place of 'their old teacher'; he refused ('fiat experimentum in corpore vili')
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 (some offered to sacrifice themselves for their old teacher)
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 translation
notes: Good 'choice' beat: 'His students begged to go instead. He said no.' 'Begged' is a touch strong: 'offered' is the record.

exact_claim: Two days later (9 Oct) he had colicky pains and moderate diarrhoea, which lasted until about 15 October; he took no medicine and felt otherwise well
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901 ('watery diarrhoea ... very slight as compared with typical cholera')
source_2: S5 SRF 2015 (9 Oct; several days of 'Bauchgrimmen und Durchfall')
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892
notes: Say: 'Two days later: stomach cramps and diarrhoea. About a week. But no cholera collapse.' No toilet imagery.

exact_claim: His stools were full of living comma bacilli (an 'almost pure cultivation')
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901
source_2: S2 Mendelsohn 2001 (millions of bacilli in his gut for over a week)
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 ('swarming with comma bacilli')
notes: Phrase cleanly: 'Lab tests showed the germs were thriving inside him.' Show a microscope slide, not stool.

exact_claim: He did not get ill at all
source_1: L1 Wikipedia ('nor did he become unwell')
notes: Wrong. He had about a week of cramps and diarrhoea (C19).

exact_claim: His pupil Professor (Rudolf) Emmerich repeated the experiment on 17 October 1892, with the same set-up; his colic and diarrhoea were much more severe, but he too survived
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901 (both he and his pupil Emmerich)
source_2: P3 Arch Hyg 1893 ('von mir und Emmerich eingenommenen')
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 ('much more severe')
notes: Good twist beat: 'His student tried it ten days later, and got much sicker.' First name Rudolf: BnF authority + Wikipedia; fine for description.

exact_claim: Emmerich needed medical help and recovered in under two weeks
source_1: S12 Huxley (popular)
notes: Not in BMJ / J Hyg. Say only 'much sicker'.

exact_claim: Others repeated the drink: Élie Metchnikoff in Paris (unharmed, but one volunteer fell gravely ill) and six people at Stricker's institute in Vienna (none developed cholera)
source_1: S13 Nautilus / Smithsonian (Metchnikoff)
source_2: S12 Huxley; archive.org b20410232 reprint (Vienna, six persons)
primary_source: Metchnikoff, Annales de l'Institut Pasteur 1893; Stricker, Studien zur Cholerafrage 1893 (not seen)
notes: Keep OUT of the Short (side plot, weak sourcing). Usable as a comment reply if someone asks.

exact_claim: He said that in his view the comma bacillus in the gut does not produce the cholera poison by itself; local conditions (the 'y') must be attended to
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901 ('considered ... that the experiment confirmed his views')
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 ('show conclusively ... does not produce the specific poison'); P3 Arch Hyg 1893 ('in dem y allein liegt der epidemiologische Schwerpunkt')
notes: Say: 'He declared victory: germs alone don't cause cholera.' Always pair with C26 and C33.

exact_claim: His critics said he had simply had a mild case of cholera; he cited the physicians Professor Bauer and Dr von Ziemssen to deny it
source_1: S4 Burnett 2009 (most epidemiologists not persuaded)
source_2: S5 SRF 2015 / S10 PZ 2025 (Koch's supporters' counter-arguments)
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 (rebuts the objection with Bauer and von Ziemssen)
notes: Say: 'His critics said: that WAS cholera, just a mild case.'

exact_claim: Names of the witnesses who saw him drink
notes: No source names them. Bauer and von Ziemssen are cited about his illness, not as witnesses to the drink. Show anonymous colleagues.

exact_claim: Quote: 'Even if I were mistaken and the experiment endangered my life I should look death calmly in the face, for it would be no thoughtless and cowardly suicide: I should die in the service of Science as a soldier on the field of battle.'
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 (German: 'denn es wäre kein leichtsinniger Selbstmord, ich stürbe im Dienste der Wissenschaft')
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 (J.S.H.) English translation of his written account; German original MMW 1892 not seen
dispute_status: wording: 'field of battle' (J Hyg) vs popular 'field of honour'
notes: Use the J Hyg wording: 'I would die in the service of science, like a soldier on the field of battle.' Do NOT say 'field of honour' (not found in any source read). Drop 'suicide' word for ad safety.

exact_claim: Koch's own personal reaction to the experiment
notes: No source read records Koch's direct response. Say 'Koch's side' / 'his critics', never 'Koch said'.

exact_claim: Why he survived (1): he had a real but mild cholera infection, or was lucky; many infections are mild
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 ('schlicht Glück')
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892 (critics' objection)
notes: Leading modern view. Say: 'Most experts now think he did catch cholera, just a mild case.'

exact_claim: Why he survived (2): the culture had weakened while grown in the lab (or Gaffky sent a weakened culture)
source_1: S5 SRF 2015 (bacteria weakened during lab cultivation)
source_2: S14 Friedmann, 'Escherich and Escherichia' (unclear whether Gaffky sent a fully virulent or weakened culture; via search excerpt, not read in full)
primary_source: P3 Arch Hyg 1893 (Pettenkofer: 'vollvirulent'; tested on animals by Gruber in Vienna)
notes: Only as 'some think the germs had weakened in the lab'. Pettenkofer insisted they were fully virulent.

exact_claim: Why he survived (3): he was immune from an earlier cholera infection
source_1: S10 PZ 2025 (listed among Koch supporters' arguments)
notes: No source documents that he had cholera earlier (e.g. 1854). Do not use on screen.

exact_claim: Modern volunteer studies: neutralising stomach acid with bicarbonate lowers the dose of cholera needed to cause disease from about 10^8 to about 10^4 germs
source_1: S15 Cash RA et al., J Infect Dis 1974;129:45-52
notes: Irony beat: 'The baking soda didn't protect him. It made the experiment MORE dangerous.' Keep numbers off screen. Never imply a safe way to do it.

exact_claim: Why he survived (4): Koch deliberately sent harmless bacteria / a student secretly boiled the culture / his excitement raised his stomach acid
source_1: S10 PZ 2025 (lists these as counter-arguments of Koch's supporters)
notes: No evidence. Period-polemic or legend. Do not use.

exact_claim: Why he survived (5): the bicarbonate dose was too small to neutralise the acid
notes: No source found proposing this. Do not use.

exact_claim: History's verdict: he was wrong that drinking water does not spread cholera; but his sanitation work (sewers, clean water) helped Munich, and some epidemiologists credit his germ-plus-environment model
source_1: S17 Evans AS 1985 Rev Infect Dis (an 'error in enteric epidemiology')
source_2: S3 Morabia 2007; S4 Burnett 2009 ('wrong side of history', but a multifactor model)
primary_source: P1 J Hyg 1901 ('whether rightly or wrongly'; typhoid almost disappeared in Munich)
notes: End beat: 'He lost the argument. But he was not all wrong: clean soil and sewers did save Munich.'

exact_claim: He gave the talk on 12 November 1892 to the Munich medical society; the British Medical Journal reported it on 19 November 1892
source_1: S4 Burnett 2009
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892;2(1664):1132, 'Professor von Pettenkofer on Cholera'
notes: A newspaper / journal-page insert is a good visual (PD).

exact_claim: His Hygiene Institute in Munich opened on 19 April 1879; LMU calls it the world's first
source_1: S18 Max von Pettenkofer-Institut history page (opening 19 Apr 1879)
notes: Say 'his famous Hygiene Institute'. Exact 1879 address not verified.

exact_claim: He drank it in his laboratory at the Hygiene Institute
notes: No source says where in Munich. Broth was prepared by institute doctors (Pfeiffer, Eisenlohr), so a lab setting is plausible: show 'a Munich laboratory' without naming the room.

exact_claim: He predicted he would not become seriously ill
notes: Single popular source. Implied by his theory, but not quoted. Skip.

exact_claim: He wrote the experiment might have been fatal if done in Hamburg (where local conditions favoured cholera)
source_1: S4 Burnett 2009
primary_source: P2 BMJ 1892
notes: Optional: shows his logic. 'He said: in Hamburg, this might have killed me.'

exact_claim: His bacilli-laden stools drained untreated into the river Isar and no cholera followed downstream
primary_source: P3 Arch Hyg 1893 ('Myriaden von Kommabacillen')
notes: True per his own report, but cut for advertiser safety (gross).

exact_claim: He died in 1901 (by suicide)
source_1: S1 J Hyg 1901 ('sudden end while in a fit of deep depression')
notes: Keep OUT of the story per brief. Do not mention.
